title: Geographical Distribution of Exposure to Fires in the United States Between 2004 and 2023
content:
Abstract

Fire activity is increasing across the United States. Proximity to fires poses health risks beyond smoke exposure including injury, mental health impacts, and contamination of water and soil. However, the predominance of smoke-focused studies has contributed to public health strategies centered on mitigating smoke exposure. This study aims to characterize geographic patterns of population-weighted fire burden to inform public health and fire management. Population-weighted fire-day burden (person days) were calculated for each census tract and year by multiplying the tract population by number of days with at least one satellite-detected active fire. This metric captures the frequency of detected fire presence, including recurrent smaller fires, rather than smoke, fire intensity, or fire severity. These measures were summarized nationally, by region, and by demographic groups. Temporal trends between 2004 and 2023 were evaluated using regression models, and region-specific percentiles identified census tracts with fire days in the 99th percentile every year (i.e., consistently high). Between 2004 and 2023, there were 9.12 billion population-weighted fire-days in the United States, 64% of which occurred in the South. Population-weighted fire burden increased significantly over the study period nationally and in most census tracts. Census tracts with persistently high fire-day burden were concentrated in Florida, consistent with regions where frequent agricultural burning occurs. Population-weighted fire burden is disproportionately high among individuals residing in the South, highlighting the importance of tailoring strategies for mitigating the health risks of fires to local fire practices to protect the health and safety of residents in the region.
